resources.string: Each side starts with sixteen pieces. White moves first, then you alternate turns.
Every piece moves its own way: bishops on diagonals, rooks in straight lines, knights in an L, the queen in any line.
Move onto an enemy piece to capture it. Pawns move forward but capture diagonally.
Attack the enemy king so it cannot escape. That is checkmate, and it wins the game.
Chess grew out of an Indian game called chaturanga, described around the 6th century. The queen and bishop took their long-range moves in southern Europe in the late 1400s.
Each player starts with twelve pieces on the dark squares. Pieces move one square diagonally forward.
To capture, jump over an enemy piece into the empty square right behind it.
If a capture is available you must take it, and you can keep jumping in the same turn.
Reach the far row to be crowned a king, which can move backward too. Capture or block every enemy piece to win.

In 2007 a research team announced that 8 by 8 checkers is solved: with perfect play from both sides it ends in a draw. Games of the draughts family were already played on chessboards in medieval Europe.
Players take turns placing a disc of their colour on the board.
A move must flank one or more enemy discs in a straight line between your new disc and another of yours.
Every flanked disc flips to your colour. If you have no legal move, you pass.
When neither player can move, the colour with more discs on the board wins.
Reversi was published in England in the 1880s. A version with a fixed starting position was sold in Japan in the 1970s under the name Othello.
Each player owns the row of pits nearest them and the store at their right.
On your turn, pick up all the stones from one of your pits and sow them one by one, counter-clockwise.
Land your last stone in your store, or in an empty pit of your own, for a bonus.
When one side runs out of stones, the game ends. The player with the most stones in their store wins.
Mancala is a family of hundreds of sowing games played across Africa and Asia. The word comes from an Arabic term meaning to move.
Take turns dropping a disc of your colour into any column.
The disc falls to the lowest empty space in that column.
Line up four of your discs in a row: across, up and down, or on a diagonal.
Block your opponent as you build your own line. If the board fills up, it is a draw.
Milton Bradley released Connect Four in 1974. In 1988 two researchers independently showed that the first player can always win with perfect play.
The board is a grid of dots. On your turn, draw one line between two neighbouring dots.
Complete the fourth side of a box to claim it. It gets your colour.
Claiming a box earns you another turn, so keep going while you can.
When every box is claimed, the player with more boxes wins.
The game was described in 1889 by the French mathematician Édouard Lucas, who called it la pipopipette. Strong players win by deciding who is forced to open the long chains of boxes.
Players take turns marking an empty square with X or O.
Get three of your marks in a row to win: across, down, or diagonally.
Block your opponent when they have two in a row.
If the board fills with no line, the game is a draw.
With best play from both sides, tic-tac-toe always ends in a draw. Three-in-a-row games on a scratched board were already played in ancient Rome.
Each player draws a hand of tiles. The tiles show two numbers of dots, one on each half.
Play a tile that matches a number at either end of the chain on the table.
If you cannot play, draw from the boneyard if tiles remain, or pass.
Go out first by playing your last tile, and score the dots left in your opponent\'s hand.
Dominoes reached Europe in the 1700s, and a Chinese version of tile games is older still. A standard double-six set has 28 tiles, one for every pairing of numbers from zero to six.
Each turn, place tiles from your rack in a single row or column to spell a word.
Your first word must cover the centre star. Later words must connect to words already on the board.
Letter and word bonus squares multiply your score, and rarer letters are worth more.
Draw new tiles after each turn. The highest score when the tiles run out wins.
Lettered-tile word games became a favourite family pastime in the mid 1900s. Letter values are set by rarity, so common letters score little and awkward ones score a lot.
Each player starts with seven cards. Flip the top card of the deck to begin the discard pile.
On your turn, play a card that matches the top card\'s colour or number, or a matching action card.
Skip, Reverse, Draw Two and Wild cards change who plays next and how. If you cannot play, draw a card.
Call UNO when you have one card left. Empty your hand first to win the round.
UNO was created in 1971 by Merle Robbins, a barber in Ohio, and first sold from his shop. The name is the word for one in Spanish and Italian, which you call out when you have a single card left.
Build four foundation piles from Ace up to King, one pile for each suit.
On the tableau, stack cards in descending order, alternating red and black.
Tap the stock to turn over new cards when you run out of moves.
Move kings into empty columns. Clear every card onto the foundations to win.
This is Klondike, the version most people know as Solitaire. It became a worldwide habit in 1990 when it shipped with Windows 3.0, where it also taught many people how to use a mouse.
The game picks a hidden word and shows a blank for each letter.
Guess one letter at a time. A correct letter appears in every place it belongs.
A wrong letter adds a part to the hanging drawing.
Reveal the whole word before the drawing is finished to win.
Versions of Hangman were being played by the 1890s, and it needs nothing but paper and a pencil. Good guessers start with common letters such as E, A and T.
A grid of letters hides a list of words.
Words can run across, down, or diagonally, and some are written backward.
Drag across the letters of a word to select it.
Find every word on the list to finish the puzzle.
The word search was first published in 1968 in a newspaper in Oklahoma. It remains one of the most common puzzles in newspapers and activity books.
Tap a square to choose a clue. Across and down clues share letters where they cross.
Type your answer. The number of squares tells you the length of the word.
Crossing words help: a letter you know from one answer can unlock another.
Fill every square correctly to complete the grid.
The first modern crossword appeared in the New York World newspaper on 21 December 1913, made by Arthur Wynne. It was diamond shaped and called a word-cross.
Guess the hidden five-letter word in six tries.
Type a real five-letter word and submit it.
Green means the right letter in the right place. Yellow means the letter is in the word but elsewhere. Grey means it is not in the word.
Use the colours to narrow down the answer before you run out of tries.
Word Guess follows the format of Wordle, made by the software engineer Josh Wardle and released in October 2021. The New York Times bought it in January 2022.
Fill the grid so every row contains the digits 1 to 9 once.
Every column must also contain 1 to 9 once.
Every 3 by 3 box must contain 1 to 9 once as well.
Use the starting numbers as clues. Each puzzle has exactly one solution.
The modern Sudoku was first published in 1979 in a US magazine as Number Place. It was renamed Sudoku in Japan in 1984 and became a worldwide craze in the 2000s.
Fill an N by N grid with the numbers 1 to N so no number repeats in any row or column.
Heavy lines divide the grid into cages. Each cage shows a target number and an operation.
The numbers in a cage must combine, using that operation, to give the target.
Work from small cages and single-cell cages outward until the grid is full.
KenKen was invented in 2004 by the Japanese maths teacher Tetsuya Miyamoto as a way to help his students practise arithmetic. The name means cleverness squared.
Fill the white squares with digits from 1 to 9.
The clue above or beside a run of squares gives the sum those digits must reach.
No digit may repeat within a single run.
Cross-check each square against its row run and its column run until the grid is solved.
Kakuro is sometimes called the crossword of numbers. It appeared in US puzzle magazines in the 1960s under the name Cross Sums and was later made popular in Japan.
Numbers beside each row and above each column describe runs of filled squares.
A clue of 3 1 means a run of three filled squares, then a gap, then one filled square.
Fill squares you know are filled and mark squares you know are empty.
Complete every row and column to reveal the hidden picture.
Nonograms were invented independently in 1987 by Non Ishida and Tetsuya Nishio in Japan. They are also known as Picross and Griddlers.
Tap a square to uncover it. Your first tap is always safe.
A number shows how many of the eight neighbouring squares hold a mine.
Use the numbers to work out where mines are and flag them.
Uncover every safe square without tapping a mine to win.
Minesweeper came to millions of desks as a free game in Microsoft Windows in the early 1990s. Its numbered clues can always be reasoned out as a logic puzzle, apart from the occasional forced guess.
The board is a grid of lights, some on and some off.
Tap a light to toggle it and its neighbours above, below, left and right.
Plan your taps: each press changes up to five lights at once.
Turn every light off to win, using as few taps as you can.
Lights Out was released as a handheld electronic game by Tiger Electronics in 1995. Mathematicians study it with linear algebra, which can tell whether a given board is solvable.
The tiles are scrambled with one empty space.
Tap a tile next to the gap to slide it in.
Put the tiles back in order, usually from 1 upward, row by row.
Plan several moves ahead: finishing one row can undo another.
The 15 puzzle caused a craze in the United States and Europe in 1880. Exactly half of all possible scrambles can be solved, which is why a puzzle with two swapped tiles is impossible.
You start in the top-left corner, which is one colour region.
Choose a colour. Your whole region changes to it and absorbs touching squares of that colour.
Grow your region by picking colours that match many neighbours.
Fill the entire board with one colour within the move limit.
Flooding a region with a colour is the same flood-fill idea behind the paint-bucket tool in image editors. Good solutions plan which colour to take next so that each move absorbs the most squares.
Each tile has coloured or patterned edges.
Tap a tile to rotate it, and drag tiles to swap their places.
Touching edges must show the same colour or pattern.
Arrange the whole board so every pair of neighbouring edges matches.

Edge-matching puzzles are known in computer science as NP-complete, meaning no fast general method is known for solving large ones. The Eternity II puzzle of 2007 offered a two million dollar prize and its deadline passed unclaimed.
The computer hides a secret code of coloured pegs.
Make a guess by placing a row of coloured pegs.
A black marker means one peg is the right colour in the right place. A white marker means the right colour in the wrong place.
Use the markers to deduce the code before you run out of guesses.

Mastermind was invented in 1970 by Mordecai Meirowitz, an Israeli telecommunications expert. In 1977 the computer scientist Donald Knuth showed that the classic four-peg, six-colour game can always be cracked in five guesses.
Drag left and right to move the paddle along the bottom.
Bounce the ball upward to knock out bricks.
Catch falling power-ups for help, and do not let the ball fall past the paddle.
Clear every brick to finish the level.
Atari released Breakout in 1976 as a one-player cousin of Pong. It inspired many later brick-breaking games.
Enemies march along a path in waves. Do not let them reach the exit.
Spend your coins to build towers beside the path.
Different towers have different range, speed and damage, so mix them.
Defeating enemies earns more coins. Survive every wave to win.

Tower defence became hugely popular in the late 2000s, partly through fan-made maps for Warcraft III and through browser and phone games. Its core idea is placement: where a tower stands matters as much as which tower it is.
Drag your mallet to hit the puck across the table.
Aim to knock the puck into your opponent\'s goal at the far end.
Defend your own goal by keeping your mallet between the puck and the slot.
The first player to reach the target score wins.

Air hockey was developed in the late 1960s by a group of engineers at the Brunswick company and went on sale in the early 1970s. The table blows air through tiny holes so the puck floats with almost no friction.
On your turn, roll five dice. You can roll up to three times.
Tap dice to hold them and re-roll the rest.
After your last roll, score the dice in one empty box on the scorecard.
Fill all thirteen boxes. Five of a kind scores a Yahtzee. The highest total wins.

Edwin S. Lowe bought the rights to the game in the 1950s from a couple who called it the Yacht Game, and he trademarked the name Yahtzee in 1956. A Yahtzee, five dice all alike, is rare: it comes up about once in 1,300 single rolls of five dice.
Each player has fifteen checkers and moves them around the board in opposite directions.
Roll two dice. Move one checker for each number, or one checker for both.
You cannot land on a point held by two or more enemy checkers. A single enemy checker can be hit and sent to the bar.
Bring all your checkers home, then bear them off. The first to bear off all fifteen wins.
Games like backgammon were played in the ancient Near East thousands of years ago. The doubling cube, which lets players raise the stakes, was added in New York in the 1920s.
Swipe in any direction to slide every tile as far as it can go.
When two tiles with the same number touch, they merge into one with their sum.
A new tile appears after every move.
Keep merging until you build the 2048 tile, and keep going for a higher score.
2048 was made in March 2014 by Gabriele Cirulli, then a 19-year-old Italian developer, and spread quickly across the web. It was inspired by earlier games such as 1024 and Threes.
Steer the snake by swiping or using the on-screen controls.
Eat food to grow longer and score points.
Do not run into the walls or into your own body.
Plan your route: the longer you grow, the less room you have.
Snake started with arcade games of the 1970s, such as Blockade. It reached a huge audience in 1997 when it came pre-installed on Nokia mobile phones.
Dots of the same colour appear in pairs around the board.
Drag from one dot to its partner to draw a path.
Paths cannot cross or overlap each other.
Connect every pair and fill every square of the board to solve it.
Connect-the-pairs puzzles with non-crossing paths are a long-standing paper puzzle type, sometimes called Numberlink. Solving them is a classic challenge for computer search programs too.
Tiles are stacked in a pattern. A tile is free if nothing is on top and it can slide out to the left or right.
Tap two free tiles with the same picture to remove them.
Flowers match any flower, and seasons match any season.
Clear all the tiles to win. Use hints or shuffle if you get stuck.
Mahjong Solitaire is a single-player game that borrows the tiles of Chinese mahjong. Brodie Lockard wrote an early computer version in 1981, and the game became widely known as Shanghai in the 1980s.
Open the tool you need: dice, coin, spinner, timer or score keeper.
Pick how many dice, or how many sections on the spinner.
Tap to roll, flip or spin, and read the result aloud for the table.
Use the score keeper and timer to run board games and party games of your own.
A standard six-sided die is numbered so that opposite faces always add up to seven. Dice have been used in games for thousands of years.
Players take turns placing a stone of their colour on an empty point of the board.
Stones never move and are never captured once placed.
Be the first to line up five stones in a row: across, down, or diagonally.
Block your opponent\'s open lines of three and four while you build your own.
The name comes from the Japanese for five points. Researchers have shown that on a 15 by 15 board with no extra restrictions, the first player can force a win.
Hex is played on a board of hexagons. One player owns the two opposite red sides, the other the two blue sides.
Take turns placing a stone on any empty hexagon.
Connect your two sides with an unbroken chain of your stones.
A game of Hex can never end in a draw, so there is always a winner.

Hex was invented by Piet Hein in 1942 and independently by John Nash in 1948. It is a known result that the first player can win with perfect play, though the winning strategy is not known for large boards.
Each player has nine pieces. Take turns placing them on the points of the board.
Form a mill, three of your pieces in a straight line, to remove one enemy piece.
After all pieces are placed, slide a piece along a line to an adjacent empty point.
Win by reducing your opponent to two pieces or leaving them with no legal move.
Boards for Nine Men\'s Morris have been found carved into stone in places across Europe, including church cloisters from the Middle Ages. In 1993 the game was shown to be a draw with perfect play.
One player controls the hare. The other controls the hounds.
Take turns sliding a piece along a line to a neighbouring empty point.
The hounds may only move forward or sideways, never backward, and try to trap the hare.
The hounds win if the hare cannot move. The hare wins by slipping past them to the far side.
Hare and Hounds belongs to the family of hunt games, where the two sides are unequal in number and goals, like Fox and Geese. Its simple rules show how a small board can still hold real strategy.
The star-shaped board has six corners. Each player starts with a set of marbles in one corner.
On your turn, move one marble to an adjacent empty hole, or hop over a neighbouring marble.
You can chain several hops in one turn, jumping over any marbles, yours or not.
Be the first to move all your marbles into the opposite corner.
Despite the name, Chinese Checkers was invented in Germany in 1892 as Stern-Halma, a star-shaped version of Halma. It was marketed as Chinese Checkers in the United States in the late 1920s.
Each player has four tokens waiting in their home base.
Roll the die. You need a six to bring a token onto the track.
Move tokens around the track by the number rolled. Landing on an opponent sends their token home.
Bring all four tokens into your home column to win. A six gives an extra roll.
Ludo is the Latin word for I play. It was patented in England in 1896 and is a simplified version of the much older Indian game Pachisi.
Shogi is Japanese chess. Each side has twenty pieces, and the pieces all face forward.
Each piece moves in its own way. Most pieces that reach the far three rows may be promoted.
Captured pieces change sides. Instead of moving, you may drop a captured piece onto any legal empty square.
Checkmate the enemy king to win.
Shogi is thought to descend from the same Indian game as chess, chaturanga. The drop rule, where captured pieces rejoin the board for the captor, is what makes shogi games so sharp and rarely drawn.
Minishogi is a small shogi played on a 5 by 5 board with five pieces per side.
Pieces move as in shogi. A piece that reaches the last row can be promoted.
Captured pieces change sides. You may drop one onto an empty square instead of moving.
Checkmate the enemy king to win. Games are short, so every move counts.
Minishogi was designed around 1970 as a quick way to learn the ideas of shogi on a small board. Even on 25 squares, the drop rule keeps the game tactical and surprising.
